title: Review: Charge and current; Semiconductors and conduction models; Potential difference and emf; Resistance and I–V characteristics; Resistivity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL11-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; EL03-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL03-uk1#t4 term and clue written for the game; EL01-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL01-uk1#N.8, EL02-1#N.6, EL03-1#N.11, EL03-uk1#N.6, EL04-1#N.4, EL01-uk1#N.6, EL02-1#N.12, EL03-1#N.3a, EL03-uk1#N.10, EL04-1#N.6a, EL01-uk1#N.4, EL02-1#N.3a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Number density
items.clue: Count of mobile particles per m³; about 10²⁹ in copper.

items.label: Reverse bias
items.clue: Way round that gives only a tiny current: very high resistance.

items.label: NTC thermistor
items.clue: Semiconductor component whose resistance falls as temperature rises.

items.label: Free electrons
items.clue: Carriers in a metal moving randomly at about 10⁵–10⁶ m s⁻¹ with no net flow.

questions.stem: A silver wire and a copper wire are connected in series, so they carry the same current. Silver has 5.9 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³; copper has 8.5 × 10²⁸. The silver wire has twice the cross-sectional area of the copper wire. What is the ratio (drift speed in silver) / (drift speed in copper)?
questions.explanation: v = I/(nAe), and I and e are the same, so v ∝ 1/(nA). Ratio = (8.5/5.9) ÷ 2 = 0.72.

questions.stem: Predict first. A cell has an emf of 1.5 V. What does this mean?

options.text: The cell holds a store of 1.5 C of charge, which it releases into the circuit.
The cell pushes each coulomb of charge around the circuit with a force of 1.5 N.
For each coulomb passing through the cell, 1.5 J is transferred to electrical energy.
The cell drives a current of 1.5 A through any circuit connected to it.

questions.stem: A student investigates whether a length of metal wire obeys Ohm's law. At the highest currents, V/I is clearly larger than at low currents. What is the best change to the method?

options.text: Use a voltmeter with a higher resolution, so the pd readings are more precise.
Take each reading twice, once with the supply reversed, and average the results.
Extend the range to even higher currents, so that more points lie on the graph.
Keep currents small or use a water bath, so the wire's temperature is constant.

questions.explanation: Ohm's law applies at constant temperature. Small currents (or a water bath) stop the wire heating, so V/I stays constant for an ohmic wire.

questions.stem: A copper wire has a fixed pd across it. As it warms up, the current falls. A student explains: "Warming reduces the number of free electrons in the copper." Which correction is right?

options.text: The student is right: fewer free electrons means a smaller current.
The wire expands as it warms, so it is longer and has a higher resistance.
The number of free electrons hardly changes; the ions vibrate more, so collisions slow the electrons' flow.
Warming gives the electrons more energy, so they move faster and fewer pass each second.

questions.explanation: Correct. More ion vibration means more frequent collisions. With the same number of carriers moving along more slowly, the current falls: R has risen.

questions.stem: A uniform copper wire is cut into two pieces of equal length. How do the resistance and the resistivity of one piece compare with those of the original wire?

options.text: Its resistance and its resistivity are both halved.
Its resistance and its resistivity are both the same.
Its resistance is the same, but its resistivity is halved.
Its resistance is halved; its resistivity is unchanged.

questions.stem: A copper wire of diameter 1.6 mm carries a steady current of 3.0 A. Measurements show that its free electrons, each with a charge of magnitude e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, drift at 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. What is the number of free electrons per unit volume in the copper?
An electron, initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of 2.0 kV. What kinetic energy does it gain, in joules?
Predict first. What is the origin of the electrical resistance of a metal wire?

options.text: Free electrons collide with the vibrating lattice ions, transferring energy to them.
Some of the free electrons are absorbed by the metal atoms, so fewer leave than enter.
The electrons rub against the surface of the wire, like water flowing along a pipe.
The electrons bump into one another as they crowd through the wire.

questions.stem: An NTC thermistor senses the temperature inside a fridge. After the door is closed, the thermistor cools from 15 °C to 5 °C. What happens to its resistance, and why?

options.text: It falls, because its ions vibrate less, so the carriers collide with them less often.
It rises, because fewer charge carriers are freed, outweighing the fewer collisions.
It rises, because its ions vibrate more as it cools, so there are more collisions.
It does not change, because a component's resistance is fixed when it is made.

questions.explanation: Cooling a semiconductor frees far fewer charge carriers. This outweighs the drop in collisions, so the resistance of an NTC thermistor rises.

questions.stem: A copper cable has length 5.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm. The resistivity of copper is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is the resistance of the cable?

A wire consists of two sections made of the same metal and joined end to end. The diameter of section 2 is half the diameter of section 1. The wire carries a steady current, which is the same in both sections. What is the ratio v₂/v₁ of the drift speed of the free electrons in section 2 to that in section 1?

options.text: v₂/v₁ = 1
v₂/v₁ = 2
v₂/v₁ = 4
v₂/v₁ = ¼

questions.explanation: The current, the number density and the charge are the same in both sections, so drift speed ∝ 1/A. Half the diameter gives (½)² = ¼ of the area, so the electrons drift 4 times as fast.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.50 A flows through a small electric motor for 2.0 minutes. In this time, 360 J of energy is transferred from electrical energy to other forms in the motor. What is the potential difference across the motor?
